title: Flash Feedback: There's a Way to Tame the Feedback Monster ew-book-flash-feedback
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: This piece is Dave Stuart Jr.'s foreword to Matt Johnson's book Flash Feedback: Responding to Student Writing Better and Faster – Without Burning Out, framed as a meditation on the 'feedback monster' — the ever-growing stack of student papers that haunts writing teachers. Stuart traces the emotional arc of new writing teachers who enter the profession to help students find their voice, only to be worn down by the sheer time cost of giving thorough feedback, a burden he notes was already being lamented in English Journal back in 1912. He recounts the origin of his friendship with Johnson and Johnson's rise from blogger to published author, using it to vouch for the book's credibility and years of research behind it. The core argument is that feedback doesn't have to mean burnout: Johnson's book offers a path to giving feedback that is efficient, effective, and humane, organized around chapters on efficiency, effectiveness, motivation, and student ownership. Stuart closes by tying the piece to his companion post on occupational burnout, urging English teachers and department chairs to make time for the book despite its unfortunate release timing amid COVID school closures.
points: The 'paper load' problem for writing teachers is not new — Stuart cites an English Journal article from 1912 lamenting the same burden, framing feedback fatigue as a century-old structural problem in the profession rather than a personal failing.

Johnson's Flash Feedback is structured around four practical levers — efficiency, effectiveness, motivation, and student ownership — giving teachers a concrete framework rather than just sympathy for the feedback burden.

Stuart explicitly links this foreword to his companion piece on occupational burnout, positioning unmanaged feedback workload as a direct driver of teacher burnout and the book as a practical countermeasure.

The personal origin story of a chance pub lunch in Cedar Springs, Michigan is used to establish Johnson's credibility and the years of grassroots blogging and research behind the book, not just marketing claims.
The central reframe — that feedback can be done efficiently and humanely — challenges the assumption that thorough feedback and teacher sustainability are inherently in tension.
quotes: All the teachers I know got into the work because they wanted to promote the long-term flourishing of young people by way of helping them master the disciplines.

But then we got into our first teaching gigs, and we taught our students to write those first essays or stories or poems, and all of a sudden a new character entered our personal stories: a stack of papers.
I love that Matt finds, in the earliest edition of the English Journal, an article lamenting the weight of the writing teacher's paper load. This was in 1912.
Within a year, Matt's blog was being read by thousands of readers each month, his work was being featured on Edutopia, and he was in talks with Corwin Literacy for a book contract.
And as Matt shares, there's a way to do this work that doesn't require us to make peace with the paper monster. There's a way to do feedback well, and to do it efficiently, and to do it humanely.
For Matt Johnson — and for all of us now, thanks to Matt's book — flash feedback isn't just a theory. It's a reality.
What Matt's well-researched book helps us do is think well about things like efficiency (Chapter 1), effectiveness (Chapters 2 and 3), motivation (Chapter 4), and student ownership (Chapter 5).
